title: Onboarding prompt labs and runloop recipes - notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working-notes doc for a small set of interactive prompt labs and runloop recipes intended for new SDK users (engineers + ML engineers). Goal is not a full quickstart — instead focused, 30–45 minute guided labs that teach: streaming responses, safe retries, cache-friendly prompts, and deterministic eval hooks.

Audience and success criteria:
- Persona: backend engineers shipping a chat/assistant feature; some familiarity with REST/gRPC and Node/Python.
- Success metrics: user completes at least 3 labs in under 45 minutes; 75% of participants can implement streaming + retry pattern in a sandbox app without instructor help.

High-level lab list (sequenced):
1) hello-stream: consume streaming tokens, render partial responses, and add a typing indicator. (15–20m)
   - Learning objective: streaming API shape, cancellation, backpressure basics.
   - Key exercises: connect SDK stream; display tokens as they arrive; cancel mid-response.
   - Edge-case note: demonstrate small latency vs. throughput tradeoffs by toggling chunk_size/flush.

2) safe-retries-and-idempotency: implement idempotency keys + deterministic replays for partially-failed requests. (20–30m)
   - Learning objective: when to retry vs fallback to cached answer; idempotency design for generation requests.
   - Exercise steps: simulate network blip; observe partial output; implement client-side idempotency header; use server-side dedupe route stub.

3) prompt-chunking-and-kv-cache lab: prefix caching for multi-turn chat and LRU cache for heavy prompts. (25–30m)
   - Learning objective: how to reuse KV cache & prefix to cut cost; when chunking helps vs hurts.
   - Tasks: instrument token counters; run with and without prefix caching and record token delta.

4) runloop-recipes: building a robust runloop that handles tools, function calls, and model fallbacks. (30–40m)
   - Learning objective: architecting the request/decision loop that routes to cheaper/fast models first and falls back to higher quality variants.
   - Recipe steps: stub tool invocation (search/file-read); detect hallucination heuristics (low-token-repetition, fact-check step); route to fallback with same conversation state.

Lab mechanics and templates:
- Each lab folder will contain: README.md (1 page quick start), steps.md (ordered tasks), solution/ (complete example app in Python + Node), small dataset for eval, and a short video (2–4 min) walkthrough.
- Timeboxing: include a 5-minute "fast path" that shows the minimal code to get something working, and a 15-minute "deep path" for best practices.
- Failure-mode section at end of each lab: top 5 debugging tips.

Runloop recipe sketch (single-file pseudocode to show decisions):
- Start with cheap model "gpt-mini" for parsing user intent + tool detection. If tool confidence >= 0.85, run tool and return result. Otherwise call mid-tier model with prefix cache and streaming enabled. If response_quality_score < threshold OR eval-run fails (regression test in-line), escalate to high-quality variant and mark telemetry for later inspection.

Prompts & prompting patterns to teach (examples):
- System prompt templates for safety + hallucination reduction (short checklist).
- Few-shot scaffold: show tokens vs examples tradeoff; prefer dynamic example selection for long contexts.
- Cache-friendly prompt design: place stable instructions in system/meta, volatile context in prefix so KV cache can be re-used.

Quick code snippet (illustrative, minimal):
- Node pseudo: create client, open stream, render tokens, on error attempt single retry with same idempotency key, if retry fails call fallbackModel().

Open questions / unresolved items (notes-to-self):
- Decide exact model names and tiers for labs (hosted vs local quantized). Need input from serving-runtime team.
- How to surface telemetry hooks in the SDK lab without requiring enterprise Console access? Option: provide a local dummy telemetry endpoint.
- Should we include a lab specifically around embeddings + semantic search connector? Pros: many teams need it. Cons: scope creep.

Teacher notes / facilitator script (bullet style):
- Start with 5-minute context: why streaming & runloops matter for product economics (latency, unit cost).
- Demo fast path in 3 minutes.
- For each pair of exercises, have one instructor-led walkthrough and then a 10–12m pair-programming window.
- Encourage measuring token counts and latency — add a scorecard to each lab.

Scoring / evaluation checklist (for participants):
- Can open stream and render tokens: Y/N
- Implemented idempotency header: Y/N
- Observed token count reduction using prefix cache: Y/N
- Can invoke fallback model and preserve chat history: Y/N

Suggested telemetry events to capture in labs (local-friendly):
- request_start, request_end, tokens_consumed, model_variant, retry_count, fallback_used, stream_cancelled
- Provide a small aggregator script that reads a local JSONL log and prints simple metrics (p95 latency, avg tokens).

Accessibility and dev-ex environment notes:
- Provide Docker dev image to avoid system setup issues (Python 3.10, Node 18, local mock server).
- Keep external dependencies minimal; avoid requiring cloud creds for labs.

Rollout plan (MVP -> GA):
- MVP: 3 labs (hello-stream, safe-retries, runloop-recipes), solution code + README, internal playtest w/ 10 engineers (2 weeks).
- V1: add prompt-chunking lab, video walkthroughs, sample telemetry aggregator, publish in docs site.
- GA: include slide deck, automated grading harness, public sample apps, translation notes for other languages.

Task checklist (next actions):
- [ ] Lock model variants with serving runtime (owner: Jared)
- [ ] Create Docker dev image + mock telemetry endpoint (owner: Evan)
- [ ] Draft README + steps.md for each lab (owner: Aisha)
- [ ] Build minimal video walkthroughs (owner: Sofia)
- [ ] Schedule internal playtests and gather feedback (owner: Aisha)

Related tickets/links (work-in-progress):
- ENG-1247: streaming SDK polish
- DOCS-452: lab pages template
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-examples/pull/318 (starter stream example)

Notes to self (style + voice):
- Keep lab READMEs lightweight: 1) TL;DR code, 2) Why it matters, 3) Steps, 4) Debug tips.
- Prefer runnable samples over long explanation pages; short videos help retention.
- Avoid heavy reliance on Console; labs should be runnable locally.

End of notes.

-- Aisha
